passage:
Gurpreet and I have shared this flat for two years, and I've never seen her like this.
She's up at 3 am most nights; I hear the kettle. Her laptop stays open on a document she closes the moment I walk past. Last week, on the phone to her mother, she kept saying, 'No, Mummy, everything's fine at work,' and then sat on the balcony for an hour afterwards.
Yesterday she asked me, out of nowhere, 'If someone got fired for complaining, do you think other companies would ever hire them?' I said I didn't know. She laughed, but it wasn't a real laugh.
She's stopped going to her team's Friday dinners. When I asked why, she said, 'They'd rather not hear what I'd say.'
I don't know what's going on. I just know she's carrying it alone.

qa.q: What time is Gurpreet up most nights?
qa.a: She's up at 3 am most nights.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet's question about being hired again suggest she fears?
qa.a: It suggests she fears losing her job and being shut out of her field if she complains.

qa.q: How could the flatmate support Gurpreet at this stage?
qa.a: The flatmate could gently mention the sleepless nights, offer to listen without pushing, and suggest Gurpreet talk the options over with someone trusted.

qa.q: How does the narrator experience watching Gurpreet?
qa.a: The narrator is worried and unsure, seeing clear signs of strain without knowing the cause, and sensing that Gurpreet is carrying it alone.

grounding: It shows, through a flatmate's eyes, a young woman losing sleep over fears of job loss and blacklisting and pulling away from colleagues.

passage:
Monday: Indu opened a blank email to the compliance team and typed the subject line: Concern about project funds. Then she thought of the home loan she had signed in January, and her father's hospital bills she was helping with. She saved it as a draft.
Thursday: she mentioned it, vaguely, to Payal over lunch. Payal set down the fork. 'Don't. Remember Arvind? He complained, and now no one in this city will hire him. Keep your head down.' Nobody else at the table looked up.
Saturday: at 2 am Indu was still awake, reading stories of people who had spoken up and lost everything. Her father called at nine to ask about her week. 'All good, Papa,' she said, and hung up feeling more alone than she had ever felt at work.

qa.q: What subject line did Indu type?
qa.a: She typed 'Concern about project funds'.

qa.q: Why did Indu save the email as a draft?
qa.a: She feared the cost of speaking up, thinking of her home loan and her father's hospital bills.

qa.q: What could help Indu at this stage before deciding?
qa.a: Talking it through with one trusted person, perhaps outside the office, would ease her isolation and help her weigh the risks calmly.

qa.q: What might Payal be feeling when warning Indu about Arvind?
qa.a: Payal is probably afraid too and wants to protect Indu, though the warning leaves Indu even more isolated.

grounding: It shows fear of job loss, blacklisting and family worries keeping a young woman awake and alone, with colleagues unwilling to speak.

passage:
In the research lab at the university in Pune, Dolma stared at her screen at midnight, the fridges humming. She had the proof now: the professor's funded study reported results from experiments that had never been run. Her own logbook showed it.
And now the fear arrived in full.
If she reported it, she would lose her position; the professor sat on every hiring panel in their small field. Her parents in Kalimpong had borrowed to support her research dreams. Her younger brother's fees depended on her stipend.
She had slept four hours a night for two weeks.
Ira, at the next bench, knew too. When Dolma raised it, Ira only said, "Don't. Please. We'll both be finished."
Dolma looked around the empty lab. Twelve people worked here. Not one would stand beside her. She had never felt so alone in a room full of equipment she knew by heart.

qa.q: What did the professor's study report?
qa.a: Results from experiments that had never been run.

qa.q: What is Dolma feeling at midnight in the lab?
qa.a: Dolma feels frightened, sleepless and deeply alone, weighing her career and family against the truth.

qa.q: What could ease Dolma's isolation before any decision?
qa.a: Talking confidentially to a trusted mentor outside the lab, or the university's research integrity office, about her options.

qa.q: What is Ira afraid of?
qa.a: Ira fears that speaking up will finish both of their careers, which is why she begs Dolma not to.

grounding: A young researcher with proof of falsified results feels the full weight of possible costs, loses sleep and feels alone as colleagues stay silent.

passage:
Zubin bhai,
I haven't told Mummy-Papa any of this, so please keep it between us for now.
You know about the accounts I found at the builder firm. I'm now sure the flat buyers' deposits were moved to another company. I have copies. And I'm terrified.
If I report it, I'll lose this job, and word travels fast in real estate; nobody else in Indore would hire me. Papa retires next year. We planned on my salary for Chotu's college. I keep imagining the office gossip, the partners' faces, being called a traitor.
I've been lying awake till three most nights. I can't eat properly. At work I smile at everyone and feel sick. Not one colleague will even talk about it; they change the subject.
I know staying quiet is wrong. Three hundred families paid for those flats. I just don't know if I'm brave enough.
Can you call me on Sunday?
Jahnavi

qa.q: How many families paid for those flats?
qa.a: Three hundred families.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi feeling most nights?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels terrified and alone, lying awake till three, torn between fear of the costs and knowing silence is wrong.

qa.q: What support could Zubin offer on Sunday?
qa.a: Listen without pushing, help think through the fears, and encourage speaking to a trusted professional about safe options.

qa.q: What might Zubin feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Zubin would likely feel worried and protective, and proud of Jahnavi's honesty.

grounding: A young employee who has found diverted deposits fears losing the job and the family's plans, loses sleep and feels alone.

passage:
Rekha, I haven't slept properly in three weeks. You asked, so I'll tell you.
At the food company, I found that the lab reports for the baby cereal had been edited. The real ones showed contamination above the limit; the ones sent to the regulator didn't. I've kept copies.
Every night I run through it. If I speak, I lose my job. The industry's small; I'd be the one nobody hires. My mother's surgery is in March, and my salary pays for it. My manager is the one who edited the reports, and also the one who got me this job.
The worst part? I hinted to two colleagues. Both went silent and walked away. I'm completely alone with it.
But then I see mothers in the supermarket with that box in their trolley. So yesterday I messaged the company's product-safety line, anonymously, with one copy, asking them to hold the batch. I'm Shreya, and I'm still scared out of my mind.

qa.q: What did the real lab reports show?
qa.a: Contamination above the limit.

qa.q: What does Shreya feel after hinting to colleagues?
qa.a: Shreya feels isolated and frightened, left completely alone when both colleagues walked away.

qa.q: What step has Shreya already taken, and what could come next?
qa.a: An anonymous message to the product-safety line asking to hold the batch; next, confidential advice and formal channels, using the copies.

qa.q: What might Rekha feel while listening?
qa.a: Rekha likely feels alarmed and protective, wanting to support Shreya through a frightening choice.

grounding: An employee who found edited safety reports fears job loss and family hardship, loses sleep and feels alone, yet takes one protective step.

passage:
Sunday: Chetan sat on the balcony at 2 am with the printed emails in a folder, the proof that his company had been overstating its sales to the bank that lent it money. Mahima found him there. "Again?" He nodded. He couldn't stop picturing the HR office, the security guard taking his badge.
Wednesday: at lunch, he quietly asked his closest colleague whether he'd noticed anything odd in the quarter-end figures. The colleague looked away. "Don't drag me into this, Chetan." Chetan ate alone after that, feeling like the office had become glass.
The next Saturday: Mahima's mother asked about his promotion. Chetan smiled and changed the subject, thinking of the home loan and his daughter's school fees. That night Mahima said, "Whatever you decide, tell me first. We'll face it together." He held her hand tightly, too tired to answer, but for the first time in weeks he didn't feel completely alone.

qa.q: What time was Chetan sitting on the balcony on Sunday?
qa.a: Chetan sat on the balcony at 2 am.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling after his colleague looked away?
qa.a: Chetan felt alone and anxious, as if the whole office had become glass and no one would stand with him.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Chetan now that Mahima has spoken?
qa.a: Chetan can share the full picture with Mahima and, with her support, look into proper channels and qualified advice before deciding how to raise the false figures.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima to watch Chetan through these weeks?
qa.a: Mahima is worried and probably frightened too, but she chooses to stand with him and asks only to be told first.

grounding: Shows the fear of losing a job, family worries and isolation weighing on a would-be whistleblower, with lost sleep and few colleagues willing to speak.
